lesson_title: Valley or Spur? Watch Which Way the V Points
hook_text: Two V shapes on your map. They look identical. One is a valley, one is a spur, and the examiner wants to know which.
clip_script: On a topographic map, valleys and spurs both make V-shaped contour lines. Same shape. Opposite landforms. Here is how you never mix them up. Valleys point to the source. Spurs point to the sea. A river carves a groove into the hill. A contour line has to stay at the same height, so it walks up into the groove, crosses the river, and comes back out. That makes a V pointing uphill, towards the source. A spur is a finger of high ground sticking down into the valley. The contour wraps around the end of it, so the V points downhill, towards the sea. Check with the numbers. Heights getting bigger towards the point? Valley. Getting smaller? Spur. Blue river running through the V's? Valley, for sure. And while you are there: rings inside rings is a hill, long thin rings a ridge, and the pinched waist between two tops is a nek, where the road crosses.
visual_style: Two identical V contour patterns side by side; one fills with a blue river and arrows pointing uphill to a mountain source, the other lifts into a 3D finger of land with arrows down to the sea; labels with heights tick up and down; quick flashes of rings, a ridge and a nek.
pacing: Fast hook, slow on the contour walk, rapid check, quick tour of the other shapes.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for hills, ridges, saddles and reading a whole landscape from contours.
